reverse_outline.summary: Three-point preview: the common shorthand is tested against dated records, the records show build order rather than split territory, and each claim is labelled by source strength
Two dated facts that cut against the usual picture: Adyen buying outside platforms right after boasting of one stack, and Stripe operating its own limited-purpose bank
Why the bank-vs-API shorthand was untested so far, earlier parts showed differences without their origin + why it matters to Larkfield, which splits volume across both providers
Statement of the reading under test and its verdict: holds for banking and hosting, fails for European acquiring, untestable on motives; the real pattern is opposite build orders converging
Evidence rules: dated company sources, separating documented, reported and inferred claims, meaning of 'not public', and the unequal quality of the two firms' figures
Roadmap of the five chapters and why the cases precede the comparison
Preview of the Stripe case: API first then a per-market regulated layer, volume but no revenue disclosed, what a small team can borrow, Larkfield tracks acquiring entity
Preview of the Adyen case: acquiring license then banking licenses, audited figures, self-declared platform edges, Larkfield keeps a small ledger without a license
Preview of the side-by-side comparison: two differences of kind (holding money, running infrastructure), the rest narrowing differences of degree, a dated answer for Larkfield's CEO
Preview of the three contrast cases (PayPal/Braintree, Checkout.com, Block), the tentative inference about permissions following first customers, and Larkfield owning both customer relationships
Preview of the closing chapter on current shifts (agents, stablecoins, instant payments) with release-phase labels, Larkfield triaging proposals, and closure of the book
Advice to read the chapters in order, the expected end-state understanding of convergence, and the starting point

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.draft_locus: all units except Chapters in this part ¶2 and ¶3
results.finding: The outliner's summaries of the callout, Introduction ¶1 to ¶5, chapter paragraphs 1, 4 and 5 and Where to Begin match the controlling ideas of their aligned spec paragraphs.

results.quote: Larkfield's payments team of 11 keeps a small ledger and seeks no license.
results.finding: p07's controlling idea includes 'two purchases closed on 1 July 2026' and 'the practices transfer and the assets do not'. The draft paragraph drops both. Without the transfer clause the Larkfield sentence has no stated link to the chapter (flowA item 12 calls it a non sequitur), and the Adyen chapter's 2026 acquisitions, which AC-1's expected answer names, are not previewed for that chapter.

results.quote: The rest are differences of default, sequence or degree that narrowed in 2025 and 2026.
results.finding: p08's controlling idea (and P10-3) sorts the comparison into three kinds, the third being 'questions not decidable from the public record'. The draft gives only two kinds, so the comparison chapter is previewed without its undecidable category, which is a third of the part's verdict.

The only unit marked two_ideas (¶2: why the shorthand was untested, and why it matters to Larkfield) is one idea and its stake; the spec's p02 controlling idea joins the two deliberately. No other unit is marked.
The opening units set up and state the part thesis; each chapter paragraph previews the chapter that argues P10-1 to P10-5 in order; the conclusion ties them into one test. No unit is orphaned.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶2 to ¶5, Chapters in this part, Figure 1, Figure 2
results.finding: Both figures carry captions saying what they show; the Stripe 'not a bank' quotation is set against the bank in the acquirer list in the same sentence; chapter-paragraph figures are framed by the bold question each chapter asks.

results.quote: Fourteen days later Adyen announced that it would buy Talon.One, a loyalty platform, for €750 million, and on 11 June that it would buy Orb, a usage-billing platform, for $335 million. Both deals closed on 1 July.
results.finding: The Adyen quotation and the two purchases are given without any sentence saying what they show (per the spec, 'a sentence about a company overtaken by that company's own acts within three months'). The next paragraph says only that 'neither fact fits' the bank/API shorthand, which is a different point and does not fit the Adyen fact (flowB item 3). Both flow readers had to infer the tension.

results.spec_locus: p02, p03, p04, p05, sections/0, p07, p08, p10, conclusion
results.draft_locus: all boundaries except Chapters in this part ¶3 -> ¶4
results.finding: Contrast ('Neither fact fits'), problem_solution ('So Part X ... tests one reading'), elaboration ('A verdict of that kind depends on how the evidence is read'), sequence ('Five chapters carry the test, in this order'), contrast ('a company that built in the other order'), conclusion_summary ('sets the two records side by side'), time ('takes the positions as fixed in November 2026') and the conclusion's summary opening are all expressed at their boundaries.

results.quote: [[payment-contrast-cases]] tests that reading on three companies that started elsewhere
results.finding: The spec's carries_over is 'the comparison's reading, traced to each company's first customers from two cases only'. The comparison paragraph before it never mentions first customers, so 'that reading' has no clear antecedent (comparison's result or the original shorthand?), and the first-customer inference then appears only as a disclaimer. Both flow readers reported this (flowA item 13, flowB item 9).

Both readers describe the order as puzzle -> claim -> method -> map, then the chapters in reading order (records, comparison, tests, outlook), which agrees with the declared large_to_small with prerequisite_order for the chapters; no section's position is unclear to either reader. Points both readers raised but judged not material: 'MALPB' unexpanded (glossed at once as 'a limited-purpose bank of Stripe's own'), Part IX's 'two vocabularies' (the audience has read Part IX), and 'Each case' before the cases are named (both call it small).

results.quote: Both deals closed on 1 July. Stripe's treasury documentation says "Stripe is not a bank."
results.finding: The opening stacks four dated facts and never says what the reader should notice in them (a 'single platform' claim followed by two purchases; 'not a bank' followed by its own bank). Both readers had to re-read or wait for the figure caption to see the point of the hook.

results.quote: By 2026, as the two opening facts show, each was moving toward the other's position.
results.finding: The Stripe half is clear (it got a bank); the Adyen half is not, because the page has not yet said that Stripe's position includes a suite assembled partly by purchase (that appears only in the case-stripe paragraph). 'Position' is undefined, and the callback in Where to Begin inherits the vagueness.

results.quote: Of eight bets, two are differences of kind
results.finding: 'Bet' is the part's title word and the comparison's organising unit, but the page never says what counts as a bet; both readers stopped on it ('the bets compared one by one', 'eight bets').

results.quote: That a provider holds the permissions its first customers required is my inference, and three cases cannot prove it.
results.finding: The contrast chapter's hypothesis arrives as a disclaimer after the examples, never introduced as what is being tested, and the paragraph's 'tests that reading' points elsewhere; readers could not tell which claim the chapter tests.

results.quote: Larkfield turns out to own the relationship with both the studio and the member.
results.finding: The Larkfield beat has no stated link to the contrast cases (the spec's point is that this is the one row the cases add: who owns the payer and who the seller, which made K8 possible). Both readers called it a non sequitur.

results.quote: Four interface practices transfer to a small team; about 2,000 database shards do not.
results.finding: Neither the practices nor the shards are named or framed, so readers could not tell what lesson the sentence carries; naming the practices in a few words (or saying 'the scale does not') would fix it.

results.quote: Sources are cited in each chapter; this introduction makes no factual claim of its own.
results.finding: On a page that states €750 million, $335 million, 28 May 2026, $1.9 trillion and 439 million accounts and insists every claim carries its source, the sentence reads as a contradiction. The spec's intent is narrower (no claim the chapters do not make and cite); the wording should say that. Only flowA reported it (minor). Not a position issue, so the house-format waiver does not apply.

The does_not_know items are handled: the companies' dated records are only named, the evidence labels and the different nature of the two companies' figures are explained in Introduction ¶4, and the three-way verdict is stated in ¶3. 'Acquirer', 'e-money institution' and 'limited-purpose bank' are glossed in place.

results.quote: the bets compared one by one
results.finding: 'Bet' is used as a term of art (the part title, 'eight bets') with no gloss; it is not in the audience's already_knows. One clause defining a bet as a lasting architectural or commercial choice would do.

results.quote: 84% of that volume was "full-stack", its own term
results.finding: The draft flags 'full-stack' as Adyen's term but does not say what it means, so the 84% cannot be read; the intro reader also could not interpret it. A few words (Adyen acquiring and processing the payment itself) would fix it.

The prose opens on two dated, sourced facts, not on a definition, a generality or 'in this part'. The KEY POINTS callout before it is the book's required opening block and is where the spec places the thesis statement.

Short, gives a reason for the order, a callback and a concrete first step; not a bare restatement or 'in conclusion' summary, though its middle sentence nearly repeats Introduction ¶3's last sentence (flowA item 15).

results.quote: The five chapters are one test and are best read in order, because the comparison rests on the two records before it.
results.finding: The synthesis ('one test', read in order) is present, but the spec's so-what (faced with a sentence about a provider, ask who documented it, when, under which definition and what the record does not say) is absent from the conclusion, as is the p11 clause that a reader with one question can enter at the matching chapter and find the same rule there. The so-what appears only in KEY POINTS bullet 3.
'By the end the two opening facts read as steps in one direction' calls back to p01 in one clause, leaving the full callback to chapter 50 as the spec decides.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶5 and Chapters in this part
results.finding: The cold reader named all five chapters in the promised order (Stripe case, Adyen case, bets compared, three contrast cases, what is moving and the book's close) with the reason for the order, matching the roadmap promise.

intro-reader.md names the five chapters in order with what each examines, states the tested claim (Adyen owns the regulated money path, Stripe the developer's abstraction) and its verdict, and lists the evidence rules: dated, documented / widely reported / inferred / not public, 'not public' not proof of absence, Stripe's unaudited figures against Adyen's audited ones, each case ending with what the record could not establish. Gaps against expected are small: under the Adyen chapter the reader does not list the 2026 acquisitions or 'what transfers', and for the comparison does not mention undecidable questions; both trace to draft omissions recorded under reverse_outline_matches_spec (p07, p08).

The first prose paragraph opens on the 9 April 2026 Adyen press release and then the Stripe acquirer list naming its own limited-purpose bank, with no general description of either company before them. The KEY POINTS bullets that precede the prose state the reading under test, which the spec places there by design; they are not a company profile.
